<reason>Both sides were disciplined and grounded, but CON built the stronger structural case and drove it through every round. A's core dilemma — the motion either duplicates negligence/consumer/sector law where cases are easy (known, cheap-to-block failures, which A showed existing doctrine reaches) or imposes a retroactive spec where cases are hard — was never squarely escaped. B asserted a "gap" but never mechanized why negligence fails in its own parade case; "renaming the duty negligence doesn't close the gap" was conclusion, not argument. A's pressure questions forced B into defining foreseeability via the provider's own evals, and A's Rebuttal 2 converted that answer into the debate's sharpest unanswered point: a regime that taxes diligent red-teaming, exempts whoever doesn't look, and frees the first victim of every new failure class. B's closing re-asserted "visibility is contemporaneous" without engaging that perverse incentive, and B never touched the open-source-publication-as-liability-event point. B's best sustained offense (user-as-deployer) was real but partially answered, and B missed the chance to exploit the tension between A's "no settled standard" and "negligence already works" claims. A's closing crystallized the choice cleanly. A's Rebuttal 1 clipping is a genuine execution cost, but the argument survived substantially intact, and A's superior adaptation, sharper rebuttals, and more live routes at the end earn a clear win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2: answering B's pressure questions with calibrated concessions ("I deny the mechanism, not the responsibility"), then turning B's own foreseeability definition into the diligence-tax attack — red-team thoroughly and author your own liability; skip testing and stay clean — a point B's closing never answered, plus the framing "PRO's best example is exactly where the motion adds nothing."</best_rebuttal>
